name: Dark Lavender
lede: Dark Lavender is a muted, greyed purple, a shade down from [[lavender]] and classed by two older systems as a pale reddish purple.

sections.title: The name
sections.body:
The swatch sits in Ridgway's 1912 plate XLIV, under a hue the plate calls 61 triple-prime, tone b, and the ISCC-NBS system of 1955 places it in block 222, light purple [1]. A second, nearby Ridgway entry on plate XXXVII carries the same hue number and lands in ISCC-NBS block 228, a related moderate reddish purple [1]. Both plate readings are scans of aged printed color, so treat them as approximate [1]. The Maerz and Paul dictionary of 1930 first records a name at this position in 1905, on its plate 43, patch E6 [1].

The xkcd survey of 2010 later collected the plain descriptive phrase "dark lavender" from the public, which is the name this article uses [1]. In the ISCC-NBS system itself the block is called pale reddish purple, about 5 CIEDE2000 units from this swatch [1]. The nearest named colors on file are [[vestal]], [[vestal]] and [[catalpa]], at 3.9, 4.7 and 4.8 ΔE [1].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: Our archive finds a color near this swatch in 31 of 23,781 paintings, as photographed [2]. Claude Monet's *Stacks of Wheat (Sunset, Snow Effect)* (1890) carries the most of it, covering 45 per cent of the canvas, and Monet's own works carry it 46 times the archive's overall rate [2]. The decade around 1910 is its peak, at 8.8 times the baseline rate, and it is most common in paintings from Denmark and France [2]. Where it appears, it most often sits as a mid-tone, and the word "Grey" shares its canvases far more than chance [2]. These are photographs of aged, varnished paintings, so read the hex as a screen approximation [2].
